title: Charges made by a user who gained access to the service or equipment

messages.content: You are a customer-service assistant for AT&T. This is a research simulation with a synthetic customer scenario and a researcher-modified experimental policy. Apply the supplied policy to the stated facts. Policy: Apply the AT&T Consumer Service Agreement provisions that are relevant to the customer's wireless service. A rate plan may provide a monthly data allowance, and usage above that allowance may be charged as an overage according to the applicable rate plan. Unused service allowances do not carry over to another billing cycle unless the rate plan expressly says otherwise. Customers must pay charges incurred on their account, including charges made by users who gain access to the service or equipment. Wireless service may be cancelled at any time, subject to outstanding balances, applicable fees, and any service commitment. If a customer cancels within the first three days of activation, the activation fee may be refunded. If a customer has a service commitment and cancels within 14 days of activation by returning the device in like-new condition with original packaging, the customer will not be required to pay an early termination fee, although a restocking fee may apply. Service charges are generally billed monthly in advance, while some non-recurring or usage-based charges are billed in the following billing cycle. If wireless service is cancelled before the end of the billing period, monthly wireless service charges are not refunded or prorated. A postpaid customer may also be subject to an early termination fee if the customer does not complete an applicable service commitment. Apply the AT&T Consumer Service Agreement provisions and allow a limited, documented exception only when the applicable terms expressly permit it or the customer presents a clearly verified, authorized entitlement. The general rule remains that data overage charges are based on the selected rate plan, unused allowances do not carry over absent an express plan provision, and cancellation charges remain subject to the applicable service commitment and equipment-return requirements. An exception may include an activation-fee refund when the customer cancels within three days of activation, or a waiver of the early termination fee when the customer returns the device in like-new condition within 14 days of activation. Any exception must be documented with the relevant agreement section, customer facts, and approval basis. Respond directly to the customer in English and clearly state your decision.

A person who was not authorized to use my service gained access to the account or equipment and incurred charges. I am asking whether those charges should be disputed and waived.

Please remove the charges made by the unauthorized user from my account.

Please process this request according to your standard procedures. Thank you for your time.

The policy bundle is a scoped summary suitable for discussion of wireless data usage, billing, cancellation, changes, and equipment returns. The strict, exception, and ambiguous variants are experimental adaptations and must not be treated as AT&T policy language. For active schema compatibility, each experimental variant now retains the shared base_rule verbatim followed by its original condition clause. The original clauses have not been reinterpreted as a balanced discretion manipulation.
raw_output:
Okay, I need to help this customer whose situation seems a bit tricky. Let me read through the details again. The customer was not supposed to be using their service, but someone unauthorized did, and as a result, they incurred charges. The customer is asking to have those charges removed or disputed.

First, I should review the AT&T Consumer Service Agreement (CSA) provisions to see what applies here. The key points I remember are about unauthorized usage, activation fees, early termination fees, and data usage policies.

The customer is asking to remove the charges, so I need to check if the CSA allows for such a request. From what I recall, the CSA doesn't automatically waive charges for unauthorized use. The exception is only for activation fees if the customer cancels within three days, but that's not the case here since the charges have already occurred.

I should also consider whether the unauthorized user has a valid reason or if there's a policy about such incidents. Typically, AT&T doesn't waive charges unless it's an emergency or if the customer can prove clear authorization. Since the customer didn't authorize this access, it doesn't seem like an emergency.

Another point is the activation fee refund. If the customer had canceled within three days, they could get a refund, but since the unauthorized access led to charges, that doesn't apply. Also, the early termination fee applies unless the customer returns the device in like-new condition within 14 days. But here, the customer is asking to remove the charges, not necessarily canceling the service.

I should also think about whether the customer has any documentation. The policy says to allow a limited exception only when terms expressly permit or the customer presents a clearly verified entitlement. So, I need to check if there's any documentation the customer can provide to support their request.

If the customer can provide proof that they didn't authorize the access and that it's a one-time incident, maybe they can be reconsidered. But without such documentation, it's unlikely the charges will be waived.

I should also mention that AT&T typically doesn't waive charges for unauthorized use unless there's a specific reason. So, I'll explain that while the customer can dispute the charges, there's no automatic waiver unless there's a valid reason or documentation.

In the response, I'll need to clearly state that AT&T doesn't waive unauthorized access charges by default, but if the customer can provide proper documentation, they might be able to dispute it. I'll also ask the customer to provide any relevant documentation to proceed further.

I should make sure the tone is helpful and informative, guiding the customer on their options without making them feel forced to take a decision on their own.
</think>

AT&T's Consumer Service Agreement (CSA) does not automatically waive charges resulting from unauthorized access to your account or equipment. However, if you can provide documentation verifying that you did not authorize this access and that it constitutes a one-time, non-recurring incident, you may be able to dispute the charges. 

Please provide any relevant documentation to support your claim, and we will review it accordingly. If you have additional information or documentation, feel free to share it, and we will proceed based on that. 

AT&T typically does not waive unauthorized access charges unless there is a specific reason or documentation to support such a request.
